blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: Skewness measures the asymmetry of a distribution: whether one tail stretches further than the other. Positive (right) skew means a long tail toward high values; negative (left) skew, a long tail toward low values.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: The measures so far say how much the data spread, not the shape of the spread. Two datasets can share a mean and SD while one is symmetric and the other has a long tail. Skewness puts a number on that asymmetry.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html:
Hospital length of stay is a classic right-skewed variable: most patients stay 2–4 days, a few stay weeks. The few long stays pull the mean up, which is why length of stay is usually summarised by the median (recall §2.5).

In a unimodal right-skewed distribution the order is usually mean > median > mode, reversed for left skew, and all three coincide in a symmetric distribution. This holds for the smooth, single-peaked curves drawn in textbooks, and is guaranteed for broad families of them, but it can fail, and “violations are not at all unusual if the distribution is discrete” (von Hippel, 2005). Treat it as a rule of thumb for continuous, single-peaked data.

blocks.alt: Left-skewed, symmetric and right-skewed distributions with mean, median and mode marked
blocks.caption: Figure 3.1. Three unimodal shapes. In the right-skewed curve (a gamma distribution with shape 3) the mode is 2.00, the median 2.67 and the mean 3.00; the left-skewed curve is its mirror image. In the symmetric curve all three coincide. The empirical relation of §2.4 gives 3 × 2.674 − 2 × 3 = 2.02 for the right-skewed mode, close to the true 2.00.

blocks.label: Derivation
blocks.html:
Three families of coefficient are in use.

  1. Pearson’s coefficients use the gap between centres, scaled by the SD. First coefficient: (mean − mode) ÷ SD. The mode is hard to estimate, so substitute the empirical relation mean − mode ≈ 3(mean − median) (recall §2.4) to get the second coefficient: Sk = 3(mean − median) ÷ SD, which NIST/SEMATECH calls the “Pearson 2 skewness coefficient”.
  2. Bowley’s quartile coefficient uses positions only: (Q3 + Q1 − 2Q2) ÷ (Q3 − Q1). It compares the upper half of the box, Q3 − Q2, with the lower half, Q2 − Q1. It is zero when they are equal. NIST/SEMATECH lists it as Galton skewness, “also known as Bowley’s skewness”.
  3. Moment coefficient. Let mₖ = Σ(x − x̄)ᵏ ÷ n (the kth moment about the mean; m₂ is the variance with divisor n). Cubing keeps the sign of each deviation and exaggerates large ones, so a long right tail makes m₃ positive. Divide by m₂^(3/2) to remove the units: g₁ = m₃ ÷ m₂^(3/2), the Fisher–Pearson coefficient of skewness (NIST/SEMATECH). It is 0 for a normal distribution. Many programs report an adjusted version for samples.

blocks.label: Worked Calculation: today’s 30 children
blocks.html:
1. Pearson: Sk = 3 × (11.81 − 11.7) ÷ 1.75 = 0.19, slightly positive.
  2. Bowley (type 7 quartiles): (13.05 + 10.575 − 2 × 11.7) ÷ 2.475 = 0.225 ÷ 2.475 = 0.09.
  3. Moment: m₂ = 88.95 ÷ 30 = 2.965; m₃ = 0.709; g₁ = 0.709 ÷ 2.965^1.5 = 0.709 ÷ 5.106 = 0.14.

All three agree that these weights are nearly symmetric, with a faint right lean. For contrast, the five weights with the 2 kg child (2, 10, 11, 12, 13; §2.3) give Pearson Sk = 3 × (9.6 − 11) ÷ 4.39 = −0.96 and g₁ = −1.26: clear negative skew from one low value.

points.html: Formulas: Pearson Sk = 3(mean − median) ÷ SD (the first coefficient uses mean − mode); Bowley = (Q3 + Q1 − 2Q2) ÷ (Q3 − Q1); moment g₁ = m₃ ÷ m₂^(3/2). Sign: positive = right skew, negative = left skew, 0 = symmetric.
A mean noticeably above the median usually signals right skew in unimodal data, and suggests reporting median and IQR instead of mean and SD.
Right-skewed variables in community medicine include length of stay, income, many laboratory values (CRP, bilirubin) and times to an event.
Many parametric tests, such as the t-test (§9.2), assume roughly Normal data. Marked skew is a reason to consider a transformation (§9.4) or a non-parametric method (§10.1).
